title: Soymilk
intro: Soymilk treats a favour as a possible trap rather than automatic kindness. The slick operator wants a co-performer, and the speaker's repeated refusal is an attempt to withhold the participation that makes the act work. Yet trouble draws him back, and he turns toward warning someone less experienced. The final shared dream becomes synchronized self-interest. Beneath the food jokes is a practical question: when people offer connection, what obligations and performances are they asking you to accept along with it?
reading: Refusal of indebtedness and complicity; warning a newcomer interrupts claimed indifference.

revisions.editorial-36-act-together: The refusal is to act with the person, not simply to watch them. A convincing social performance often requires somebody else to accept the role assigned to them: grateful beneficiary, loyal associate, impressed audience. The old operator's skill matters only if the speaker supplies that cooperation. Repeating 'no time' is a way of withdrawing it, although the verse admits that the disruption still forces him to spend effort.
revisions.36-phrase-favor: The worry is about owing this particular person, after recognising their acting skill. A favour can create an expectation that later limits what the recipient may refuse. Declining it is therefore not an abstract rejection of generosity. It is a judgement about the terms under which apparent help arrives. The track makes a social obligation visible before it has been accepted, while 'Debt' explores the exhausting work of collecting obligations afterwards.
revisions.editorial-36-focus-elsewhere: He claims that his attention moved on long ago, then continues by warning a newcomer about the person. That continuation gives his involvement another possible purpose besides winning his own quarrel. Even if he wants out, he does not want someone inexperienced to mistake the performance for trustworthy care. The song's indifference is selective: it refuses a manipulator while still spending words on the person who could be taken in.
revisions.36-n4: The shared sky and dream initially promise common purpose. What turns out to be synchronized is each person's private calculation. The abacus makes self-interest audible as a collective rhythm: people can move together without actually caring for one another. This closes the verse's argument about acting and favours. Agreement on a reassuring public story is not proof that the underlying obligations are mutual.
